https://www.etymonline.com/word/statistics
Statistics. Word first recorded in 1770. Referred to the science of 
collecting data about the condition of a state or community
From the German word Statistik. Popularised, possibly coined, by 
political scientist Gottfried Achenwall in his 1748 work Vorbereitung zur
Staatswissenschaft [Preparation to Statecraft]
Statistik derives from the Modern Latin phrase statisticum collegium, 
meaning a lecture course on state affairs. This is linked to the Italian 
word statista, meaning a person skilled in statecraft
Statista comes from the Latin status, meaning position, condition, 
public order, or community organisation. Status derives from stare, 
meaning to stand, which can be traced to the Proto-Indo-European root 
sta-, meaning to stand or be firm. We make our claims firm through 
statistics!!!
Statistics = statecraft
Statistics is the science of the state, 
trying to map out the “average” 
citizen, so it can control, box, and 
regulate populations
The Oxford English Dictionary notes that Achenwall did not appear to regard Statistik as a new term, although its 
current use can be traced to him
By 1829, statistics had acquired the broader meaning of numerical data collected and classified systematically. It also 
came to describe the study of subjects through extensive numerical analysis. That’s what we are going to learn in the 
next 5 weeks!
The abbreviation stats was recorded by 1961 and is now widely used in both formal and informal contexts

Correlations
Great for control
Obscuring results
Why? Because they occur so quickly
Multicollinearity!!
What correlations show us is that everything is 
related to everything else, which philosophically is an 
endearing thought because it makes us connected to 
each other and to the universe
However, everything is related to everything else,
but not in equal measures!
Correlations are weak ties
You can infer correlation from causation
but you cannot infer causation from correlation

“When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to 
everything else in the universe.” Muir, J. (1894). The mountains of 
California. New York: The Century Co.

Correlation asks whether two variables vary together, either:
When one goes up, so does the other (both go up or down)
(called a ‘positive’ correlation)
When one goes up, the other goes down (one up, one down)
(called a ‘negative’ correlation)
Correlation expresses things that co-occur, that happen together:
Mutual relationship
Covariation
Association 
For example: Low income is correlated with more frequent use of community services:
Income down and use frequency up, a negative correlation (Aand B)
However, we cannot claim that: When A, then B
Correlation does not express causation!!
An often made mistake, also in Machine Learning
Correlations
“John and Mary walk together“
“John makes Mary walk together“

Correlations
Main lesson: Correlation is not causation no matter how Big the Data are
Actually, with more data, significant but meaningless correlations are likelier to occur
We call that spurious correlations
Obesity
Cancer
Sugar intake
(not fat)
For 90% related, so what are you going to 
fight? Obesity, cancer, or both?
Why we do research:
To find the root cause of correlations
Correlations do not ‘test’ anything; they indicate relationship. You cannot infer from correlations. They 
are non-parametric measures and hence, are not meant for Hypotheses testing. For that, you need t-
tests and Analysis of Variance (Lecture 10), or Bayesian statistics (Lecture 11). Those are parametric tests

Spurious correlations
“I always have bad luck at board games. I never roll a 6.”
Recognizable? Anyone?
This is the remarkable ‘decrease effect,’ which is not so 
remarkable at all
Based on pure chance and with a fair die:
About half (½) of the players roll low (one, two, or three)
and the other half (½) roll high (four, five, six)
On a second throw, half of those high throwers throw high again: 
a quarter (¼) of the total
On a third throw it is one eighth (⅛)
On the fourth throw it is one sixteenth (1/16)
The group that consistently throws high becomes smaller and 
smaller and eventually ceases to exist (the deceasing effect)
9/66

pages.text:
Spurious correlations
“I always have bad luck at board games. I never roll a 6.”
Recognizable? Anyone?
Yet, the group that always throws low (you!) also becomes 
smaller with each throw, which we may call an ‘increasing effect,’ 
because you will throw higher than before every now and then
This increase (“ Now you will throw high!”) can ‘magically’ be 
predicted without having to roll the dice a thousand times
Beforehand, you do not know where the correlation will show 
up, only that it will show up somewhere if you include enough 
variables in the comparison
Deviations from the average are always there, so if you compare 
enough variables you will always find something that sticks 
together – a spurious correlation
Only if predictable and reproducible will you know where the correlation should appear and is it genuine

Cohen’s kappa (κ)
Measure of inter-rater reliability (or agreement) for categorical items. It is 
generally thought to be a more robust measure than simple percent agreement 
calculation since κ takes into account the agreement occurring by chance
Cohen’s kappa is used for assessing the reliability of agreement between two 
raters (or judges, observers, etc.) who each classify items into mutually exclusive 
categories. It is applicable when the data are nominal (i.e., categories do not 
have a natural order) and the number of raters is two
Cohen’s κ is one way to quantify qualitative data

α
Cronbach’s 
Takes the average covariance divided by the average total variance
For a high -value, covariance must be high relative to item variance
Thus, the relationships / consistency among questionnaire items account for 
most of the overall variability
A higher suggests that the items have shared commonality and are likely measuring the same 
underlying concept
A lower suggests that the items are measuring different constructs or that the scale is heterogeneous
Corrected Item-Total Correlations: Items correlating < .01 with the scale total should be removed from 
that scale
Cronbach’s indicates reliability and should be > .60 for new scales, and > .70 for existing scales
Cronbach, L. J. (1951). Coefficient alpha and the internal structure of tests. Psychometrika, 16, 297–334. doi: 10.1007/BF02310555

0 low level of internal consistency

Spearman’s rho (ρ) for rank-order correlations
Spearman’s rho (ρ), also known as Spearman’s rank-order correlation coefficient, 
is a nonparametric measure of the strength and direction of association that 
exists between two variables measured on at least an ordinal scale. It assesses 
how well the relationship between two variables can be described using a 
monotonic function
Spearman’s rho is used when the assumptions of the Pearson correlation coefficient are not met, 
particularly when the data are not normally distributed, when the sample size is small, or when 
there are outliers that might distort the correlation if Pearson’s r were used. It is also the 
appropriate correlation measure when the variables are measured on an ordinal scale (where the 
data can be ranked but the intervals between data points are not necessarily equal)

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Thus, PCA executes an orthogonal transformation to convert a set of observations of possibly 
correlated variables into a set of values of linearly uncorrelated variables called Principal Components. 
The number of principal components is less than or equal to the number of original variables
PCA is a means of data reduction, placing items together such that the greatest variance by any 
projection of the data comes to lie on the 1st coordinate (i.e., Principal Component 1)
The second greatest variance comes on the 2nd coordinate (i.e., Principal Component 2), etc.
PCA does not care where your items come from. It may place all items in Component 1 except for one 
item that may form Component 2 or 3 all by itself

pages.text:
Thus, Component 1 accounts for as much of the variability in the data as possible, and each 
succeeding component accounts for as much of the remaining variability as possible
PCA is used for several purposes in statistics:
Dimensionality reduction: Reducing the number of variables while retaining most of the original
variability
Data compression: Making data easier to explore and visualize
Feature extraction: Creating new uncorrelated variables that can be used in subsequent analysis
(i.e., Machine Learning)
Noise reduction: By capturing the main variance in the data, PCA can help to identify and discard noise
Multivariate data analysis: Understanding the structure of high-dimensional data
Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
The principal components represent the directions in the data that maximize variance
(i.e., the “most important“ directions)
The eigenvalues associated with each principal component indicate the amount of
variance accounted for by that component
The loadings (the coefficients of the linear combination) can be interpreted as the
weights by which each standardized original variable should be multiplied to get the
component score
55/66

Correlations. We have seen that they indicate events 
or data points that are associated, but do not say 
anything about the nature of that relationship
Because correlations are easily established, spurious 
correlations may be significant (the dice just rolled 6 
times 6) but empirically, that means nothing
Pearson Product-Moment Correlation (r) is the most 
common, used to assess the degree of relatedness on 
some dimension but also to show that data points are 
unrelated (e.g., as control, or for discriminant validity)
Cohen’s kappa (κ) and Krippendorff’s alpha () are 
typically for testing inter-rater reliabilities (e.g., in 
content analysis)

ummary
Cronbach’s is to evaluate the reliability 
(convergent validity) of the items on a psychometric 
measurement scale (#items should be ≥ 3, cut-off 
point for reliability usually > .70)
Spearman-Brown coefficient ρ (split-half) serves the 
same purpose but for #items = 2
Spearman’s rho (ρ) (rank order) is to compare lists of 
items that at least are measured on an ordinal scale 
(e.g., annual university rankings)
Convergent validity tells in how far items indicate
the same construct; divergent validity tells in how far 
items (of another scale) indicate different constructs
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) can be used to 
gauge divergent (or discriminant) validity (but 
insignificant Pearson’s r would also do the trick)

In Lecture 07: Correlations, Spearman-Brown coefficient ρ (split-half) can be used to test the 
reliability of the mean scores (M) to a 2-item psychometric scale. In the example, the average 
scores to the indicative item were M = 5 and to the counter-indicative item M = 0. Would 
split-half say this 2-item scale is reliable? Why?
Statistics is engaging
disagree  0—1—2—3—4—5  agree
Statistics is boring
disagree  0—1—2—3—4—5  agree
A
The two items show opposite averages, so there is perfect misalignment
B
Reliable. One should recode the contra-indication and then scores match
C
Unreliable. The psychological meaning of this scale is highly controversial
D
M = 5 and M = 0 gives a grand mean of GM = 2.5, scale midpoint = neutral,
so the correlation is 0
